newsitem.title: SRI LANKA: Depleted Sri Lanka army launches recruitment drive.
newsitem.headline: Depleted Sri Lanka army launches recruitment drive.

text.p: Sri Lanka's army will launch a recruitment drive this month to fill its depleted ranks but could face difficulties because of battlefield setbacks, military officials and analysts said on Tuesday.
The government may have to introduce conscription to find the required numbers for the war against secessionist Liberation Tigers of Tamil Eelam (LTTE) rebels, some analysts said.

"We're going for a one week general recruiting programme across the island outside operational areas starting June 23," said Brigadier Jayantha Ranaweera, the army's director of personnel administration. "We hope to get the maximum numbers."
The army can train 2,000-3,000 recruits at its training schools at any given time while regimental centres can train about 10,000, he said.
Recruitment to the nearly 100,000-strong army has dried up in recent years and the army has lowered physical and educational qualifications and granted repeated amnesties for deserters.
The armed forces have also begun running slick advertising campaigns on television and other media and introduced walk-in interviews in recent months to attract more recruits.

Military analysts said the Indian Ocean island's youth have become reluctant to enlist because of successive battlefield setbacks like last week's rebel raid on army defences in northern Vavuniya and mounting casualties.
"Recruitment could slow down after this latest debacle," said air vice marshal Harry Goonetileke, a former air force chief. "This setback could be enough to alarm village parents."

Military officials said the army lost up to 140 soldiers and killed 320 of some 1,000 rebels who breached army defences at Thandikulam and Nochchimodai, near the government-held town of Vavuniya, 220 km (135 miles) north of the capital Colombo last Tuesday.
The LTTE, fighting for a separate homeland for minority Tamils in the Indian Ocean island's north and east, have said more than 300 soldiers were killed along with 50 guerrillas.
Independent confirmation of the casualties is not possible since international media are not allowed into the war zone.
The rebels were trying to capture artillery and disrupt the army's latest offensive into the LTTE's northern Wanni jungle stronghold launched from Vavuniya.
Analysts said the rebels were able to overrun the defences as the positions were thinly manned and some were held by sailors and policemen because of the army's acute shortage of soldiers.
However, the raid showed that the LTTE were having their own recruitment problems as they used a large number of female fighters, analysts said.
Goonetileke, whose son was killed when the Tigers shot down the air force plane he was flying two years ago, said the government should introduce national service to overcome the troop shortage.
"National service is the only answer. Also, we should be thinking of women on the battle front," he said.
Sri Lankan President Chandrika Kumaratunga has said the government will consider introducing conscription if necessary to get the required numbers to fight the rebels.
